pr_title: Error out when struct size is bigger than int.MaxValue
pr_body:
Fixes: #97412

`sizeof()` in C# returns a signed integer. This PR is to adjust the runtime to match with that.

Added a check for struct size and a test.
pr_comments: Do we need a test?
@jkotas This PR is ready to be reviewed again.

I've pushed out a change that makes further progress in the handling within the managed type system, but the test probably still won't compile because `BigArray` with size of `int.MaxValue` gets its size bumped past `int.MaxValue` through alignment after we're done with layout (the final size needs to be divisible by pointer size and `int.MaxValue` isn't.

CoreCLR is fine with this overflowing but the managed type system isn't. I'm not sure if the overflow is an actual _problem_ but fixing it doesn't look exactly trivial.
@MichalStrehovsky Is there a way to stop the new test from being compiled by NativeAOT?

> @MichalStrehovsky Is there a way to stop the new test from being compiled by NativeAOT?

Only by placing `<NativeAotIncompatible>true</NativeAotIncomplatible>` in the project file. It would be good not to disable all existing ManagedSequential type loader testing just because the new test doesn't work (i.e. put it in a separate project file).

Note that this is the managed type system that is shared with crossgen2. Might want to run crossgen2 outerloop testing to see whether this also needs to be removed from precompilation there.

The managed type system doesn't handle this test because the size of the `BigArray` struct is actually over 2 GB when boxed (this is also true on JIT-based CoreCLR). If a 2 GB overflow is problematic, is the 2 GB overflow of that one not problematic?

@MichalStrehovsky Based on Jan's comment from earlier. Loading `BigArray` itself should continue to work. Why do we need to align `BigArray` to pointer size? If that's needed, `sizeof(BigArray)` would return a bigger value than `int.MaxValue`. Is that correct?

> The size of it gets aligned when boxing it, because it's 8 bytes larger (MethodTable pointer) and aligned. On CoreCLR today, doing:

We chatted with Fan on Teams about this and apparently the program I posted only works on a Release build (also _without_ debugger attached) and throws InvalidProgram otherwise. On .NET 8 CoreCLR-JIT. Curious.

Actually, isn't the negative size in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/97412 just a "display artifact"? ECMA-335 defines sizeof as returning an unsigned int32, but the C# compiler treats it as signed. So it looks like it overflowed, but that's just because the C# compiler incorrectly retyped the number.

Based on the discussion here: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/95193#issuecomment-1906592092, the conclusion was that the size of struct shouldn't be bigger than `FIELD_OFFSET_LAST_REAL_OFFSET`.

@MichalStrehovsky You mentioned earlier that when boxing `BigArray`, it got aligned to pointer size. That shouldn't affect the return value of `sizeof(BigArray)`, meaning the alignment due to boxing shouldn't be taken into consideration. That's implementation details related to boxing operation, not sizeof.

> @MichalStrehovsky You mentioned earlier that when boxing `BigArray`, it got aligned to pointer size. That shouldn't affect the return value of `sizeof(BigArray)`, meaning the alignment due to boxing shouldn't be taken into consideration. That's implementation details related to boxing operation, not sizeof.

In general i don't understand the reason why a int32 limit is needed here. I assume this spot also limits size of sequential layout classes. If it affects classes, why a class cannot cross this limit, why a boxed struct can. And if it doesn't affect classes, why not?

The motivation with C# sizeof feels a bit bogus because I believe that's a C# bug. I can imagine we have problens with large enough classes/structs but I'm not very confident max int32 is the limit and LAST_REAL_OFFSET has a good chance to be breaking while at the same time not being the actual problem threshold.

@MichalStrehovsky Please refer to https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/95193#issuecomment-1906592092 and the discussion above it. My takeaway after reading that discussion is that it seems to be meaningless to allow a struct of a super big size, which may cause issues later on during runtime. Let's agree on a large enough number. That is `FIELD_OFFSET_LAST_REAL_OFFSET`.
We should align NativeAOT/crossgen2 with the same behavior as CoreCLR before merging this PR.

> @MichalStrehovsky Please refer to [#95193 (comment)](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/95193#issuecomment-1906592092) and the discussion above it. My takeaway after reading that discussion is that it seems to be meaningless to allow a struct of a super big size, which may cause issues later on during runtime. Let's agree on a large enough number. That is `FIELD_OFFSET_LAST_REAL_OFFSET`.

That discussion is about size of InlineArray which was a new feature in .NET 8. What this PR is doing is adding limit to something that didn't have this limit for 22+ years (it's not a new thing like InlineArray). It is a breaking change: we better have a good justification for customers who may be broken by it. `LAST_REAL_OFFSET` feels pretty low. Real world users might be broken - this has been possible for 22 years after all and we don't know if type sizes above this limit are problematic at all.

I already wrote my opinion in the InlineArray issue that the limit should be where we have implementation limitations that may cause it to be a problem. Instead of doing that, an arbitrary limit was chosen (`LAST_REAL_OFFSET` limit is based on VMs need to steal 5 bits of field offset during type loading - which doesn't apply to the situation we're discussing and it didn't apply to InlineArray either).

At least one limitation seems to be that the C# language decided maximum size of a type is 2 GB so we could as a courtesy not allow that. `sizeof` returning a negative number seems bad enough that it _may_ justify a breaking change.

I don't think anyone has an understanding where the other implementation limitations are. Native AOT and ReadyToRun probably have a limitation around _aligned size of the type_ being over 2 GB. It's not clear if there are other limitations. Since nobody investigated the implementation limitations, what is giving us the confidence that `FIELD_OFFSET_LAST_REAL_OFFSET` is better than 2 GB? What is giving us confidence things below `FIELD_OFFSET_LAST_REAL_OFFSET` will not overflow?

That said, people make changes in this area despite my contrary opinions, that's fine, I'm not the one ultimately responsible. I can help mirroring whatever approach is decided into the managed type system and can sign off on managed type system changes. I don't review CoreCLR VM changes since I'm not expert so I don't need to be convinced on this.
@jkotas @VSadov Do you agree with the solution here?

> @jkotas @VSadov Do you agree with the solution here?

I think that the current version of the PR is unnecessary breaking change. It is rejecting a lot more than just what's required to fix the overflow.

@jkotas If choose `int.MaxValue` or anything number bigger than that. From the C# user point of view, it means somehow we allow the last field of a struct to be very big, but we don't allow that for other fields. This is a very strange behavior to me.

The CoreCLR JIT and type loader have number of internal implementation limits, maximum field offset is one of them. I agree that it can be produce non-intuitive observable behaviors if one does not know what those limits are exactly. I am not worried about it too much. These non-intuitive behaviors are only going be hit by the few folks doing low-level tricks with extremely large structs and they should be capable to figure it out.

@jkotas There is another customer opened issue which complains about this inconsistent behavior. See https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/105064 for more details. If we are fine with these kind of customer complains, then I could revert the solution back to checking if the size of the struct is smaller than `int.MaxValue` to be compliant with roslyn/C#.

> See https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/105064 for more details.

#105064 can be improved by providing a better error message (field offset too big) instead of the generic type load exception error.

My primary concern with current version of the change is that it is a breaking change. It breaks code that worked fine for last 20 years and that likely exists out there. It would need breaking change notice with a justification, etc. 

If we really wanted to reduce the inconsistencies, it would be better to do that by relaxing the type loader internal limits, without introducing breaking changes.

I think this PR should be just about fixing the `sizeof(...)` overflow problem in C#. Checking for `int.MaxValue` should be sufficient for that.
@MichalStrehovsky As discussed above, please mirror this behavior of CoreCLR for NativeAOT. It is currently failing.
@lambdageek May I get a sign-off for Mono side of change?

@MichalStrehovsky CoreCLR and Mono side of work has been completed and approved. The remaining piece of work is related to NativeAOT/Crossgen2. I am going to transfer the ownership of this PR to you, since you will be working on that.

Additionally, this could probably be merged for .NET9, as I don't think that this is a breaking change. @jkotas Please correct me, if I were wrong.

There is no rush. @MichalStrehovsky
I plan to merge this PR when main is .NET10. The managed type system part used by NativeAOT and crossgen can be worked on later during .NET10 release.

issue_context.title: The type loader has silent integer overflows
comments:
Is this really an integer overflow in the type loader? Spec for the IL sizeof instruction says the result is unsigned int32. The code generated by Roslyn treats it like it was signed so it gets formatted as signed but it wasn't.

The signedness of the value disappears on the IL evaluation stack so it's not bad IL, but still kind of wrong.

Cc @jaredpar

> Spec for the IL sizeof instruction says the result is unsigned int32

The spec for C# says it's a signed int. 🤷

That decision was so long ago, hard to say why the two disagreed here. Wonder if that was due to CLS compliance and wanting to avoid unsigned types in the language. That's just speculation. But either way, it's very explicit in the language that it's done this way.
I agree that the runtime is following the IL spec and the problem is technically in C#. I think we should make the runtime fit C# that is our primary user experience.

review_comments:
Nit: My preferred way to do overflow checks is do the calculation with higher precision and then verify that there is no information lost by truncation to the original precision:
```
long result = (long)left._value + (long)right._value;
if ((int)result != result)
   throw
```
This is universal pattern that works for all operations.
This test is good, but you should also add one with `bool` that I have shared in my comment. I expect that the test case with `bool` is still going to fail with the current version of the change.
